claim: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are essential metalloenzymes that employ sophisticated radical chemistry to reduce the 2′-OH group of ribonucleotides and thereby produce deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs), the building blocks of DNA.
source: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are essential metalloenzymes that employ sophisticated radical chemistry to reduce the 2′-OH group of ribonucleotides and thereby produce deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs), the building blocks of DNA.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical knowledge about RNRs.

claim: The reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides is the only known pathway for the de novo synthesis of dNTPs.
source: This reaction is the only known pathway for the de novo synthesis of dNTPs.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Three classes of RNRs are differentiated based on their structural features and radical generating mechanism.
source: Three classes of RNRs are differentiated based on their structural features and radical generating mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification knowledge.

claim: Class I RNRs consist of a radical generating subunit, R2 and a catalytic subunit, R1.
source: Class I consists of a radical generating subunit, R2 and a catalytic subunit, R1.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Class I RNRs.

claim: Oxygen is required to generate a radical in the R2 subunit, which is reversibly shuttled to R1 to initiate the ribonucleotide reduction.
source: Oxygen is required to generate a radical in the R2 subunit, which is reversibly shuttled to R1 to initiate the ribonucleotide reduction.
evidence: This is a statement of established mechanistic knowledge about Class I RNRs.

claim: Class I RNRs are found in eubacteria and all eukaryotes.
source: Class I, found in eubacteria and all eukaryotes, is to date divided into five subclasses, Ia–Ie, based on the type of metal cofactor, metal ligands, and radical storage in R2 (Högbom et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Högbom et al., 2020.

claim: Class I RNRs are divided into five subclasses, Ia–Ie, based on the type of metal cofactor, metal ligands, and radical storage in R2.
source: Class I, found in eubacteria and all eukaryotes, is to date divided into five subclasses, Ia–Ie, based on the type of metal cofactor, metal ligands, and radical storage in R2 (Högbom et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Högbom et al., 2020.

claim: The R2 subunit is characterized by a ferritin-like fold housing two metal ions coordinated by six conserved residues.
source: The R2 subunit is characterized by a ferritin-like fold housing two metal ions coordinated by six conserved residues (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006), that is two histidines and four carboxylates (with the exception of subclass Ie, Blaesi et al., 2018; Srinivas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nordlund and Reichard, 2006, and Blaesi et al., 2018; Srinivas et al., 2018.

claim: The six conserved metal-coordinating residues in R2 are two histidines and four carboxylates, with the exception of subclass Ie.
source: The R2 subunit is characterized by a ferritin-like fold housing two metal ions coordinated by six conserved residues (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006), that is two histidines and four carboxylates (with the exception of subclass Ie, Blaesi et al., 2018; Srinivas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blaesi et al., 2018; Srinivas et al., 2018.

claim: The class Ib R2 subunit (R2b) metal site can bind two manganese ions or two iron ions.
source: The class Ib R2 subunit (R2b) metal site can bind two manganese ions or two iron ions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about R2b.

claim: The two metal ions in R2b are oxidized from the M(II)/M(II) state to a short-lived M(III)/M(IV) intermediate which decays to M(III)/M(III) while producing a radical species on an adjacent tyrosyl residue (Tyr·).
source: The two metal ions are oxidized from the M(II)/M(II) state to a short-lived M(III)/M(IV) intermediate which decays to M(III)/M(III) while producing a radical species on an adjacent tyrosyl residue (Tyr·), where it is also stored (Cotruvo et al., 2013; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotruvo et al., 2013; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010.

claim: The tyrosyl radical is stored on the tyrosyl residue in R2b.
source: The two metal ions are oxidized from the M(II)/M(II) state to a short-lived M(III)/M(IV) intermediate which decays to M(III)/M(III) while producing a radical species on an adjacent tyrosyl residue (Tyr·), where it is also stored (Cotruvo et al., 2013; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotruvo et al., 2013; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010.

claim: The di-manganese R2b was shown to be the physiologically relevant form of R2b.
source: The di-manganese R2b was shown to be the physiologically relevant form of R2b (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Cox et al., 2010), it accumulates higher amounts of radical and has higher enzymatic activity than the di-iron R2b.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Cox et al., 2010.

claim: Di-manganese R2b accumulates higher amounts of radical and has higher enzymatic activity than the di-iron R2b.
source: The di-manganese R2b was shown to be the physiologically relevant form of R2b (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Cox et al., 2010), it accumulates higher amounts of radical and has higher enzymatic activity than the di-iron R2b.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Cox et al., 2010.

claim: Molecular oxygen (O2) can directly activate the di-iron R2b.
source: Molecular oxygen (O2) can directly activate the di-iron R2b (Huque et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huque et al., 2000.

claim: The di-manganese R2b form cannot react with O2 but requires a superoxide radical (O2•−) provided by NrdI.
source: In contrast, the di-manganese R2b form cannot react with O2 but requires a superoxide radical (O2•−) provided by NrdI, a flavoprotein which is generally encoded in the same operon as R2b (Figure 1; Berggren et al., 2014; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Roca et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berggren et al., 2014; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Roca et al., 2008.

claim: NrdI is a flavoprotein which is generally encoded in the same operon as R2b.
source: In contrast, the di-manganese R2b form cannot react with O2 but requires a superoxide radical (O2•−) provided by NrdI, a flavoprotein which is generally encoded in the same operon as R2b (Figure 1; Berggren et al., 2014; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Roca et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berggren et al., 2014; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2010; Roca et al., 2008.

claim: NrdI is a small, globular protein that binds the redox-active flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor.
source: NrdI is a small, globular protein that binds the redox-active flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about NrdI.

claim: NrdI stands out in comparison to other flavodoxins by being able to perform two successive one-electron reductions.
source: NrdI stands out in comparison to other flavodoxins, which perform single one- or two-electron transfers, by being able to perform two successive one-electron reductions (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2008.

claim: Fully reduced NrdI with hydroquinone FMN (NrdIhq) can reduce O2 to O2•− while being oxidized to semiquinone NrdI (NrdIsq).
source: Fully reduced NrdI with hydroquinone FMN (NrdIhq) can reduce O2 to O2•− while being oxidized to semiquinone NrdI (NrdIsq) (Cotruvo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cotruvo et al., 2013.

claim: NrdIsq can produce a second O2•− from another O2 molecule and become fully oxidized (NrdIox) in the process.
source: NrdIsq can in turn produce a second O2•− from another O2 molecule and become fully oxidized (NrdIox) in the process (Berggren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berggren et al., 2014.

claim: The oxidation state of NrdI can be followed by ultraviolet–visible light absorption (UV–vis) spectroscopy.
source: The oxidation state of NrdI can be followed by ultraviolet–visible light absorption (UV–vis) spectroscopy.
evidence: This is a statement of established spectroscopic knowledge.

claim: NrdI is faint yellow in the hydroquinone state, dark blue in the semiquinone state, and bright orange in the oxidized state.
source: NrdI is faint yellow in the hydroquinone state, dark blue in the semiquinone state, and bright orange in the oxidized state (Røhr et al., 2010; Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Røhr et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: NrdI binds tightly to R2b in a 1:1 ratio with FMN at the protein–protein interface, forming a dimer of heterodimers.
source: NrdI binds tightly to R2b in a 1:1 ratio with FMN at the protein–protein interface, forming a dimer of heterodimers.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the R2b-NrdI complex.

claim: Previously obtained crystal structures of the R2b–NrdI complex from Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus show that a conserved channel connects FMN and the metal site in R2b.
source: Previously obtained crystal structures of the R2b–NrdI complex from Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus show that a conserved channel connects FMN and the metal site in R2b (Boal et al., 2010; Hammerstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boal et al., 2010; Hammerstad et al., 2014.

claim: The channel connecting FMN and the metal site in R2b is proposed to shuttle O2•− produced by NrdI in complex with R2b to the metal site, where the radical is formed.
source: This channel is proposed to shuttle O2•− produced by NrdI in complex with R2b to the metal site, where the radical is formed.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural observations.

claim: Both metalloenzymes and flavodoxins are very sensitive to photoreduction during the exposure to the high-energy X-ray radiation of synchrotron sources.
source: However, both metalloenzymes and flavodoxins are very sensitive to photoreduction during the exposure to the high-energy X-ray radiation of synchrotron sources.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about X-ray crystallography challenges.

claim: Synchrotron crystal structures of RNR and NrdI proteins invariably suffer from photoreduction.
source: Synchrotron crystal structures of RNR and NrdI proteins invariably suffer from photoreduction, which complicates the determination of the oxidation state of redox-active centres and has proven to be a problem for obtaining fully oxidized structures (Grave et al., 2019; Johansson et al., 2010; Røhr et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grave et al., 2019; Johansson et al., 2010; Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: Serial femtosecond crystallography (SFX) overcomes the problem of photoreduction by the so-called diffraction-before-destruction principle.
source: Serial femtosecond crystallography (SFX) overcomes this problem by the so-called diffraction-before-destruction principle (Doerr, 2011; Nass, 2019; Neutze et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doerr, 2011; Nass, 2019; Neutze et al., 2000.

claim: Short intense X-ray pulses of the duration of only a few femtoseconds are produced by an X-ray free electron laser (XFEL).
source: Short intense X-ray pulses of the duration of only a few femtoseconds are produced by an X-ray free electron laser (XFEL), illuminating one crystal and giving rise to one diffraction pattern at a time.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about XFEL technology.

claim: SFX allows to record the scattering information before atomic displacement has time to occur resulting in a dataset effectively free from the effects of radiation damage.
source: This method allows to record the scattering information before atomic displacement has time to occur resulting in a dataset effectively free from the effects of radiation damage (Spence, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Spence, 2017.

claim: The first SFX structures of R2b in complex with NrdI in the oxidized and hydroquinone state are presented in this study.
source: Here, we present the first SFX structures of R2b in complex with NrdI in the oxidized and hydroquinone state.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The SFX datasets reveal redox-dependent structural rearrangements both in the FMN-binding pocket of NrdI and at the protein interface.
source: The datasets reveal redox-dependent structural rearrangements both in the FMN-binding pocket of NrdI and at the protein interface.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Despite the significant rearrangement in the direct vicinity of the cofactor, FMN itself changes surprisingly little between redox states.
source: Despite the significant rearrangement in the direct vicinity of the cofactor, FMN itself changes surprisingly little between redox states.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Structures of free NrdI display significant conformational change of FMN between different oxidation states.
source: This marks an interesting contrast to structures of free NrdI, which display significant conformational change of FMN between different oxidation states.
evidence: This is a statement based on comparison with previously published structures.

claim: R2b–NrdI complex formation is restricting FMN movement and inhibits conformational change with possible implications for its redox properties and O2 reactivity.
source: We conclude that the R2b–NrdI complex formation is restricting FMN movement and inhibits this conformational change with possible implications for its redox properties and O2 reactivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data and computational calculations.

claim: Quantum chemical density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to computationally estimate the strain energy and additional effects on the FMN redox properties.
source: Moreover, we performed quantum chemical density functional theory (DFT) calculations to computationally estimate the strain energy and additional effects on the FMN redox properties.
evidence: This is a statement of the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The first R2b–NrdI complex with a di-manganese metal centre from B. cereus is described in this study.
source: We also describe the first R2b–NrdI complex with a di-manganese metal centre from B. cereus.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The metal coordination in both structures blocks access to the channel that connects FMN and the metal site providing further information on gating and control of catalytic reactive oxygen species.
source: The metal coordination in both structures blocks access to the channel that connects FMN and the metal site providing further information on gating and control of catalytic reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The two structures were solved in space group C2221 and are of very similar quality with a resolution of 2.0 Å and similar unit cell dimensions.
source: The two structures were solved in space group C2221 and are of very similar quality with a resolution of 2.0 Å and similar unit cell dimensions (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The asymmetric unit contains one monomer of the 1:1 BcR2b–NrdI complex.
source: The asymmetric unit contains one monomer of the 1:1 BcR2b–NrdI complex.
evidence: This is a statement of the crystallographic structure.

claim: The physiological dimer can be generated by applying crystal symmetry.
source: The physiological dimer can be generated by applying crystal symmetry (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Clear electron density maps allowed modeling of residues 1–299 of 322 for R2b and 1–116 of 118 for NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox.
source: Clear electron density maps allowed us to model residues 1–299 of 322 for R2b and 1–116 of 118 for NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and 1–298 of R2b and all 118 residues of NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq.
evidence: This is a statement of the crystallographic structure.

claim: Clear electron density maps allowed modeling of residues 1–298 of R2b and all 118 residues of NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq.
source: Clear electron density maps allowed us to model residues 1–299 of 322 for R2b and 1–116 of 118 for NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and 1–298 of R2b and all 118 residues of NrdI in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq.
evidence: This is a statement of the crystallographic structure.

claim: BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq are similar, as indicated by the Cα root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) value of 0.16 Å.
source: Overall BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq are similar, as indicated by the Cα root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) value of 0.16 Å (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Refinement of both structures was conducted independently from each other following the same protocol with final Rwork/Rfree of 0.16/0.20 for BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and 0.15/0.18 for BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq.
source: Refinement of both structures was conducted independently from each other following the same protocol (see Materials and methods for details) with final Rwork/Rfree of 0.16/0.20 for BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and 0.15/0.18 for BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Hammerstad et al. previously reported two crystal structures of the BcR2b–NrdI complex obtained by single-crystal X-ray diffraction at a synchrotron source and under cryogenic conditions, where R2b harbours a di-iron-active site.
source: Hammerstad et al. previously reported two crystal structures of the BcR2b–NrdI complex (Hammerstad et al., 2014), obtained by single-crystal X-ray diffraction at a synchrotron source and under cryogenic conditions. Here, however, R2b harbours a di-iron-active site.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hammerstad et al., 2014.

claim: Structural alignment between the published synchrotron and XFEL structures shows that the overall fold of the complex is similar with Cα-RMSD values between 0.42 and 0.47 Å.
source: Structural alignment between the published synchrotron and our XFEL structures shows that the overall fold of the complex is similar with Cα-RMSD values between 0.42 and 0.47 Å (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Compared to the BcR2bFeFe–NrdI structures, a 7–8 residue extended ordered C-terminus for R2b is observed in the XFEL structures.
source: Compared to the BcR2bFeFe–NrdI structures we observe a 7–8 residue extended ordered C-terminus for R2b in our structures.
evidence: This is a statement of the structural differences observed.

claim: The C-terminus in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox continues in the same orientation as the C-terminal helix without keeping a helical conformation.
source: The C-terminus in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox continues in the same orientation as the C-terminal helix without keeping a helical conformation.
evidence: This is a statement of the structural observation.

claim: The C-terminus interacts with a groove between R2b and NrdI extending the R2b–NrdI-binding area by forming hydrogen bonds to two other helices of R2b and a loop in NrdI.
source: It interacts with a groove between R2b and NrdI extending the R2b–NrdI-binding area by forming hydrogen bonds to two other helices of R2b and a loop in NrdI (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reduction of free FMN causes the isoalloxazine to bend along the N5–N10 axis leading to a 'butterfly bend' where the isoalloxazine moiety deviates from planarity.
source: Reduction of free FMN causes the isoalloxazine to bend along the N5–N10 axis leading to a 'bufferfly bend' where the isoalloxazine moiety deviates from planarity (Figure 4; Zheng and Ornstein, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng and Ornstein, 1996 and Figure 4.

claim: NrdI binds one molecule of FMN noncovalently.
source: NrdI binds one molecule of FMN noncovalently.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about NrdI.

claim: The pyrimidine ring of the 7,8-dimethyl-isoalloxazine ring is buried and tightly bound to the protein by a combination of hydrogen bonds and π-stacking interactions while the benzene ring and part of the phosphate tail are solvent exposed.
source: The pyrimidine ring of the 7,8-dimethyl-isoalloxazine ring is buried and tightly bound to the protein by a combination of hydrogen bonds and π-stacking interactions while the benzene ring and part of the phosphate tail are solvent exposed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Røhr et al., 2010 presented QM/MM calculations of the theoretical butterfly bend for FMN bound to NrdI.
source: The same study also presents quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations of the theoretical butterfly bend for FMN bound to NrdI.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: The calculated butterfly bend angles for FMN bound to NrdI are shallow with −3.1° for FMNox and −3.9° for FMNsq and more pronounced with 14.1° for FMNhq.
source: The calculated angles are shallow with −3.1° for FMNox and −3.9° for FMNsq and more pronounced with 14.1° for FMNhq (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4B and citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: Røhr et al. investigated the influence of photoreduction on the butterfly bend in FMN bound to BcNrdI.
source: The authors investigated the influence of photoreduction on the butterfly bend in FMN bound to BcNrdI.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: The measured butterfly bend in the BcNrdIox+e structure (PDB ID: 2X2O) is 4.6°.
source: The measured butterfly bend in this structure is 4.6° and does thus not correspond well to the calculated FMNox or FMNsq angle.
evidence: This is a statement of the structural observation from Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: The butterfly bend of 4.6° in BcNrdIox+e resembles the calculated theoretical butterfly bend of 3.3° of the physiologically not relevant anionic semiquinone state of FMN (FMNsq−).
source: It does however resemble the calculated theoretical butterfly bend of 3.3° of the physiologically not relevant anionic semiquinone state of FMN (FMNsq−) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4B and citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: The butterfly bend in the BcNrdIsq+e structure (PDB ID: 2X2P) was 11° after data collection, similar to the calculated FMNhq angle.
source: The second NrdI structure (PDB ID: 2X2P, 1.2 Å resolution) structure was produced from protein in the semiquinone state and the butterfly bend was 11° after data collection, similar to the calculated FMNhq angle (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4B and citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: Røhr et al. could confirm the reducing effect of the synchrotron radiation on FMN by comparing Raman spectra of the crystals before and after data collection.
source: The authors could confirm the reducing effect of the synchrotron radiation on FMN by comparing Raman spectra of the crystals before and after data collection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: Johansson et al. observed the same discrepancy between the butterfly bend for a synchrotron structure of initially oxidized NrdI from Bacillus anthracis (BaNrdI), a protein with 99% sequence identity to BcNrdI and identical FMN protein environment.
source: Johansson et al. observed the same discrepancy between the butterfly bend for a synchrotron structure of initially oxidized NrdI from Bacillus anthracis (BaNrdI), a protein with 99% sequence identity to BcNrdI and identical FMN protein environment (Johansson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johansson et al., 2010.

claim: BaNrdIox+e (PDB ID: 2XOD) is even more bent than BcNrdIox+e with 5.7°, indicating significant photoreduction of FMN during data collection.
source: BaNrdIox+e (PDB ID: 2XOD, 1.0 Å resolution) is even more bent than BcNrdIox+e with 5.7°, indicating significant photoreduction of FMN during data collection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Johansson et al., 2010.

claim: The use of SFX allowed investigation of the conformation of oxidized FMN in NrdI for the first time.
source: The use of SFX allowed us, for the first time, to investigate the conformation of oxidized FMN in NrdI.
evidence: This is a statement of the primary findings of the study.

claim: In BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox, the isoalloxazine moiety of FMNox is almost planar, with a butterfly bend of 0.2°.
source: In BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox, the isoalloxazine moiety of FMNox is almost planar, with a butterfly bend of 0.2°.
evidence: This is a statement of the structural observation.

claim: The butterfly bend of 0.2° in BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox is comparable to the angle of −3.1° for FMNox in NrdI calculated by QM/MM.
source: This value is comparable to the angle of −3.1° for FMNox in NrdI calculated by QM/MM (Røhr et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison with computational results from Røhr et al., 2010.

claim: The bend of FMNhq in the BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq structure is minimal with only 0.1° and thus similar to FMNox in the BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox structure.
source: Unexpectedly, the bend of FMNhq in the BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq structure is minimal with only 0.1° and thus similar to FMNox in the BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox structure (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4A, B.

claim: An isomorphous difference (Fo(ox)–Fo(hq)) map of BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq was calculated using the phases of the oxidized dataset.
source: Additionally, we calculated an isomorphous difference (Fo(ox)–Fo(hq)) map of BcR2bMnMn–NrdIox and BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq using the phases of the oxidized dataset.
evidence: This is a statement of the computational analysis performed.

claim: Isomorphous difference maps reduce model bias by directly comparing the experimental data and are very sensitive to subtle changes of atom positions in different datasets.
source: These maps reduce model bias by directly comparing the experimental data and are very sensitive to subtle changes of atom positions in different datasets (Rould and Carter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rould and Carter, 2003.

claim: The Fo(ox)–Fo(hq) map shows a slight movement of the oxygen on C4 of FMN indicating a small twist of the pyrimidine ring between both structures but no further bending.
source: The Fo(ox)–Fo(hq) map shows a slight movement of the oxygen on C4 of FMN indicating a small twist of the pyrimidine ring between both structures but no further bending (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5.

claim: The angle of BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq does not correspond to either the calculated bend of FMN of 14.1° nor the experimental bending angle of BcNrdIsq+e of 11°.
source: This angle of BcR2bMnMn–NrdIhq does not correspond to either the calculated bend of FMN of 14.1° nor the experimental bending angle of BcNrdIsq+e of 11°.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous computational and experimental results.

claim: In the R2b–NrdI complex, the solvent exposed part of FMN is covered by R2b, which closes the binding pocket with residues Met16, Phe17, Gln20, Ile197, and Val200.
source: In the R2b–NrdI complex, the solvent exposed part of FMN is covered by R2b, which closes the binding pocket with residues Met16, Phe17, Gln20, Ile197, and Val200 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Nonpolar contacts formed between the outermost methyl groups of FMN and the side chains of Phe17 and Gln20 are sterically hindering the isoalloxazine moiety from bending.
source: In particular, nonpolar contacts formed between the outermost methyl groups of FMN and the side chains of Phe17 and Gln20 are sterically hindering the isoalloxazine moiety from bending.
evidence: This is a structural interpretation of the observed interactions.

claim: Both side chains Phe17 and Gln20 are in turn held in place through a network of interactions involving a second shell of residues from R2b and NrdI that prevent Phe17 and Gln20 from changing conformation should FMN bend.
source: Both side chains are in turn held in place through a network of interactions involving a second shell of residues from R2b and NrdI that prevent Phe17 and Gln20 from changing conformation should FMN bend (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by Supplementary file 1.

claim: DFT calculations were performed based on the R2b–NrdI complex structures or structures of NrdI alone (PDB IDs: 2X2O, 2X2P), including all first and second sphere interactions between FMN and the surrounding protein and water molecules, with around 170–250 atoms modelled quantum mechanically.
source: In order to quantify the strain effects induced by R2b on FMN, we performed quantum chemical DFT calculations based on the R2b–NrdI complex structures or structures of NrdI alone (PDB IDs: 2X2O, 2X2P), including all first and second sphere interactions between FMN and the surrounding protein and water molecules, with around 170–250 atoms modelled quantum mechanically (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the computational methods used.

claim: The DFT calculations suggest that the isoalloxazine ring of FMN is bent in NrdI, with bending angles of −2° to 11° depending on the redox state.
source: The DFT calculations suggest that the isoalloxazine ring of FMN is bent in NrdI, with bending angles of −2° to 11° depending on the redox state, which compares well with the angles calculated at the QM/MM level by Røhr et al. (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2, and comparison with Røhr et al.

claim: The binding of R2b to NrdI results in a more planar isoalloxazine ring for all oxidation states, with a bending angle of only –3° to +4°.

claim: The strain and electrostatic effects tune the redox potential of FMN by 118 mV and 54 mV in the R2b–NrdI complex relative to NrdI alone for the oxidized/semiquinone (FMNsq/FMNox) and semiquinone/hydroquinone (FMNhq/FMNsq) redox couples, respectively.

claim: The redox tuning effects arise from the combination of strain and electrostatic effects.
